questions.text: When comparing averaged immunization data from two pediatric medical groups, it is appropriate to use
questions.explanation: A t-test A t-test is the appropriate statistical test when comparing the means (averages) of two independent groups. In this scenario, averaged immunization data from two pediatric groups constitutes two group means — making the t-test the correct inferential statistical tool. Standard deviation (A) is a descriptive measure of spread within a single dataset, not a comparison tool. Chi-square (C) is used for categorical/count data — not averaged continuous data. Variance (D) is also a descriptive measure of dispersion, not a comparative test. Per AHRQ biostatistics guidance and CPHQ Health Data Analytics domain standards, the two-sample t-test is the gold-standard method for comparing means between two independent groups.

questions.text: The frequency of errors in a particular process would best be displayed in an …..
questions.explanation: Histogram A histogram displays the frequency distribution of data — how often values or categories of errors occur — making it ideal for visualizing the frequency of errors in a process. A Pareto chart (B) also displays frequency but ranks categories from most to least frequent and includes a cumulative percentage line, making it more appropriate when the goal is prioritization rather than simple frequency display. A matrix diagram (A) shows relationships between variables in a grid format. An affinity diagram (C) organizes qualitative ideas into themes — not a quantitative display tool. Per CPHQ data analytics standards, when the question asks specifically about displaying frequency of a process variable, the histogram is the direct answer.

questions.text: When assessing an emergency room, the best strategy for data collection is
questions.explanation: Continuous sampling In a high-volume, fast-paced environment such as an emergency room, continuous sampling — capturing data on every case or event as it occurs — provides the most complete and accurate picture of performance. Emergency departments have unpredictable patient volumes, highly variable case mixes, and time-sensitive quality indicators (door-to-physician time, triage accuracy, throughput) that require ongoing real-time data capture rather than periodic or selective sampling. Cluster sampling (A) groups subjects by predefined clusters and is used for large geographic studies. Matched random sampling (C) is a research design for controlled studies. Accidental (convenience) sampling (D) introduces selection bias. Per AHRQ emergency care quality measurement standards and CPHQ data collection principles, continuous sampling is the optimal strategy for ED assessment.

questions.text: In data collection, Qualitative data are to Quantitative data as
questions.explanation: Opinion are to facts Qualitative data captures subjective, descriptive, non-numerical information — such as opinions, perceptions, and experiences. Quantitative data captures objective, numerical, measurable information — facts, counts, and measurements. The analogy "opinion are to facts" correctly maps qualitative (opinion/subjective) to quantitative (facts/objective). Option C (attitudes are to deeds) partially resembles this but does not accurately capture the data type distinction — deeds are behavioral observations, not inherently quantitative. Options B and D bear no recognized relationship to the qualitative-quantitative distinction. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and standard research methodology, qualitative:quantitative = opinion:fact is the correct conceptual analogy.

questions.text: After aggregating data, it is important to summarize the information with data displays so that it is

options.b: Meaningful to those analyzing the outcomes
options.d: Publishable to the general public and in compliance with HIPAA standards

questions.explanation: Meaningful to those analyzing the outcomes The primary purpose of data display after aggregation is to communicate findings in a way that is meaningful and actionable to the decision-makers and analysts who will use the information to drive improvement. Visual appeal (A) is a secondary design consideration, not the primary purpose. Making data understandable to all employees (C) is a broader communication goal that may apply to some contexts but is not the universal purpose of analytical data displays — displays are targeted at those who will act on the data. Compliance with HIPAA and public publishability (D) are regulatory considerations irrelevant to the purpose of internal data summarization. Per IHI measurement science and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, data displays must be meaningful to those who will analyze and act on them.

questions.text: Which one of the following is NOT the description of an analysis tool?

options.a: Pareto chart: illustrates common causes or sources of problems
options.b: Run chart: Provides a running record of a process over time
options.c: Control chart: Similar to the Run chart, but includes a median data line
options.d: Scatter diagram: graphically displays the relationship between two variables

questions.explanation: Control chart: Similar to the Run chart, but includes a median data line This is the incorrect description. A control chart is not simply a run chart with a median line added. A control chart includes statistically calculated upper and lower control limits (set at three standard deviations from the mean/center line) that distinguish common cause variation from special cause variation. The center line on a control chart is the mean, not the median. A run chart uses a median line, but the control chart's defining feature is its statistically derived control limits — not a median line. Descriptions A, B, and D are accurate. Per IHI statistical process control standards, Shewhart's original control chart methodology, and CPHQ data analytics domain competencies, the control chart's defining characteristic is its statistically computed control limits, not a median.

questions.text: The CPHQ uses a run chart or control chart to find trends within a process. A trend is determined by

options.a: Seven or more consecutive ascending or descending data points with 21 or more total points
options.b: Seven or fewer consecutive ascending or descending data points with 21 or more total points
options.c: Seven or more consecutive data points all above or all below the median or mean
options.d: Unrelated points indicating a special cause variation

questions.explanation: Seven or more consecutive ascending or descending data points with 21 or more total points In run chart and control chart analysis, a trend is defined as seven or more consecutive data points that are all ascending or all descending — signaling a directional shift in the process that is unlikely to occur by chance. The requirement of 21 or more total data points ensures the chart has sufficient data to support meaningful pattern interpretation. Option B (seven or fewer) is incorrect — the rule requires seven or more. Option C describes a shift (data points above or below the center line), not a trend. Option D (unrelated points) describes noise or common cause variation, not a trend. Per IHI run chart rules, Lloyd's statistical process control methodology, and CPHQ data analytics standards, the trend rule is seven or more consecutive ascending or descending points.

questions.text: The CPHQ measures averages to locate the center point in a data group. Which statement is FALSE?

options.a: Mean calculates the frequency a number occurs and gives the most valid picture
options.c: Variance measures the distance between the extreme numbers
options.d: Standard deviation is the square root of the variance

questions.explanation: Mean calculates the frequency a number occurs and gives the most valid picture This statement is false on two counts. First, the mean does not calculate frequency — frequency is how often a value occurs, which is the domain of mode, not mean. The mean is the arithmetic average (sum of all values divided by the number of values). Second, characterizing the mean as always giving "the most valid picture" is incorrect — in skewed distributions, the median is actually a more valid measure of central tendency. Option B is also partially inaccurate (the median is the middle value, not the average), but Option A contains the most clearly false statement with the most significant clinical and statistical implications. Option C (variance measures distance between extremes) is more accurately the definition of range, not variance — however, Option A is the primary false statement tested here. Option D is correct: standard deviation is the square root of variance. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and basic biostatistics, Option A is the false statement.

questions.text: Random Variation is to Special cause of variation as

options.a: An expected outcome is to an adverse outcome
options.b: Geriatrics is to primary care medicine
options.d: A sterile field is to an operating room

questions.explanation: An expected outcome is to an adverse outcome Random (common cause) variation is the normal, expected, predictable variability inherent in any stable process — it produces expected outcomes within control limits. Special cause variation is abnormal, unexpected, and attributable to a specific identifiable cause — it produces outcomes outside expected parameters, analogous to an adverse outcome that signals something has gone wrong. The analogy "expected outcome : adverse outcome" correctly captures the relationship between common cause (normal, expected) and special cause (abnormal, unexpected) variation. Options B, C, and D present analogies from clinical medicine (specialty types and surgical procedures) that bear no conceptual relationship to statistical variation types. Per IHI SPC methodology and CPHQ data analytics standards, this analogy accurately maps the variation taxonomy.

questions.text: Secular variation of a time series is represented graphically by
questions.explanation: A trend line Secular variation refers to long-term, gradual directional movement in a time series — a sustained upward or downward trajectory over an extended period (months to years), as distinguished from seasonal, cyclical, or irregular fluctuations. This long-term directional movement is represented graphically by a trend line. Cyclic movements (A) represent recurring fluctuations over multiple years (economic cycles) — distinct from secular trend. Sporadic motions (B) represent irregular, unpredictable variation. Staying within control limits (D) describes a stable process in statistical control — not a time series variation type. Per epidemiological time series analysis standards and CPHQ data analytics domain competencies, secular variation is synonymous with trend and is represented by a trend line.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about capability analysis of a process is TRUE?

options.a: Capability analysis requires the presence of a special cause of variation
options.b: Capability analysis requires that the process is in Statistical control
options.c: Capability analysis is used to identify the limits of the current process
options.d: The degree to which the average temperature in refrigerators in a hospital falls outside specification on any given day may be displayed in a capability analysis

questions.explanation: Capability analysis requires that the process is in Statistical control Process capability analysis measures how well a process meets its specifications — but this analysis is only valid and meaningful when the process is first demonstrated to be in statistical control (i.e., exhibiting only common cause variation with no special causes present). A process with special cause variation (A) is unpredictable and cannot have its capability validly assessed — the instability must be resolved first. Option C describes the purpose of control limits, not capability analysis specifically. Option D describes an application scenario rather than a defining truth about capability analysis. Per Six Sigma DMAIC methodology, Shewhart SPC principles, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, statistical control is the prerequisite for any valid capability analysis.

questions.text: The degree to which the average temperature in refrigerators in a hospital falls outside specification on any given day may be displayed in a
questions.explanation: Control chart Temperature in hospital refrigerators is a continuous measurement tracked over time, and the question asks specifically about the degree to which the average falls outside specification — which is the domain of statistical process control. A control chart plots data over time with a center line and statistically determined control limits, making it the ideal tool to display whether temperature readings are staying within specification or falling outside acceptable bounds on any given day. A bar chart (A) compares discrete categories. A Pareto chart (B) ranks problems by frequency. A histogram (D) displays distribution of a dataset but does not track temporal variation against specification limits. Per IHI SPC methodology and CPHQ data analytics standards, the control chart is the correct answer for time-based process specification monitoring.

questions.text: The upper limit of a control chart should be

options.a: 2 Standard deviations above the center line
options.b: 3 Standard deviations above the center line
options.c: 4 Standard deviations above the center line

questions.explanation: 3 standard deviations above the center line The upper control limit (UCL) of a Shewhart control chart is set at 3 standard deviations (3-sigma) above the center line (mean). This threshold is the universal standard in statistical process control — a data point falling beyond 3 sigma has less than a 0.27% probability of occurring by chance in a stable process, making it a reliable signal of special cause variation. 2 standard deviations (A) would generate excessive false alarms. 4 standard deviations (C) would miss true signals. Per Shewhart's original SPC methodology, Six Sigma quality standards, IHI improvement tools, and CPHQ data analytics domain competencies, 3 standard deviations is the established and universal UCL standard.

questions.text: From a study of a sample of patient records for the prior 20 months, the medication error rate was found to be 1 per 1000, with a 90% confidence interval between zero and 3.4 error per 1000. What is the chance that the true value is not covered by the interval?
questions.explanation: 0.1 Calculation and Justification: A 90% confidence interval means the interval will contain the true population value 90% of the time across repeated sampling. Therefore, the probability that the true value is NOT covered by the interval is 1 − 0.90 = 0.10. This is the alpha level (significance level) associated with a 90% confidence interval. Option A (0) would imply certainty — no confidence interval provides 100% certainty. Option B (0.034) has no statistical basis in this calculation. Option D (0.9) is the probability that the interval does cover the true value — the complement of what is asked. Per AHRQ biostatistics principles and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, the probability of non-coverage equals 1 minus the confidence level: 1 − 0.90 = 0.10.

questions.text: The upper and lower control limits of a process control chart are three standard deviations from the mean. A data point that falls outside these limits

options.a: Will be found 5% of the time even if the process is in statistical control
options.b: Will be found 5% of the time even if the process is out of statistical control
options.c: Indicates the presence of a sentinel event
options.d: Is a signal for further investigation

questions.explanation: Is a signal for further investigation A data point falling outside the 3-sigma control limits is a signal of special cause variation — meaning something unusual has affected the process and warrants investigation to identify and address the assignable cause. Option A is statistically incorrect: at 3-sigma limits, a point outside the limits occurs by chance only 0.27% of the time (not 5%) when the process is in control — 5% is the threshold for 2-sigma limits. Option B is similarly incorrect and nonsensical. Option C is wrong: a data point outside control limits is a statistical signal, not a sentinel event — sentinel events are defined patient safety occurrences, not statistical findings. Per Shewhart SPC rules, IHI statistical process control guidance, and CPHQ data analytics standards, any point outside control limits is a signal requiring investigation, not automatic conclusion.

questions.text: In which of the following scenarios is rule-based sampling most appropriate?

options.b: Assessing compliance to the time-out procedure

questions.explanation: Functional testing of laboratory machines Rule-based sampling (also called criterion-based or protocol-driven sampling) applies a predefined rule to determine which cases are selected — for example, testing every machine on a scheduled cycle, or sampling every nth unit under specific triggering conditions. Functional testing of laboratory machines follows strict, predefined testing protocols and schedules — making rule-based sampling the natural fit. Obtaining customer feedback (A) uses purposive or convenience sampling. Assessing time-out compliance (B) typically uses continuous or systematic sampling of surgical cases. Measuring patient falls (C) typically involves continuous event reporting rather than rule-based sampling. Per CPHQ data collection methodology standards and laboratory quality management frameworks (CLIA, CAP), functional testing of equipment follows structured, rule-based testing schedules.

questions.text: What is the most likely effect of tampering when dealing with control charts?

options.a: Reducing variation when the process is stable
options.b: Increasing variation when the process is stable
options.c: Failing to recognize special cause variation when it is present
options.d: Falsely identifying special cause variation when none exists

questions.explanation: Increasing variation when the process is stable Tampering refers to making adjustments to a stable process in response to common cause variation — treating normal process noise as if it were a signal requiring correction. Deming demonstrated that tampering with a stable process (one exhibiting only common cause variation) paradoxically increases overall variation rather than reducing it — the adjustments themselves introduce additional variability. This is illustrated by the funnel experiment. Option A is the opposite of what tampering produces. Options C and D describe interpretation errors in reading control charts — not the effect of tampering on the process itself. Per Deming's 14 Points, IHI SPC educational resources, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, tampering with a stable process increases variation.

questions.text: A frequency plot may be used to examine
questions.explanation: All of the above A frequency plot (histogram or frequency distribution display) provides a complete picture of a dataset's distributional characteristics, revealing all three fundamental properties: the shape of the distribution (normal, skewed, bimodal), the spread (range, variance — how widely data is distributed), and the center (where the data clusters — mean, median, mode). No single option A, B, or C alone fully captures the analytical power of a frequency plot. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and basic descriptive statistics, a frequency plot is a comprehensive exploratory tool that simultaneously reveals shape, spread, and center of a dataset.

questions.text: A data inventory and a data dictionary will

options.a: Increase the need for new data elements
options.b: Increase the efficiency of the data collection process
options.c: Increase the cost of the data collection process
options.d: Result in all of the above

questions.explanation: Increase the efficiency of the data collection process A data inventory catalogs what data elements already exist within an organization, and a data dictionary provides precise operational definitions for each element. Together, these tools eliminate redundant data collection, prevent duplication of effort, ensure consistent interpretation of data elements across collectors, and streamline the collection process — all of which increase efficiency. They do not increase the need for new elements (A) — rather, they often reveal that needed data already exists. They do not inherently increase cost (C) — they typically reduce costs by preventing rework and redundancy. Per AHRQ data quality standards, NQF measurement infrastructure guidelines, and CPHQ data analytics domain competencies, data inventories and dictionaries are efficiency tools.

questions.text: An acute care facility recently revised its clinical protocol for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia. It has since experienced greater variation in monthly staff performance. The number of ventilated patients per month has remained approximately the same. When sampling medical records for the monthly review, how should the organization adjust the sample size?

options.c: Keep the sample size the same
options.d: Review the medical record of each ventilated patient until variation is reduced

questions.explanation: Increase the sample size When variation in performance increases, a larger sample size is required to detect true signals of change with adequate statistical precision. Greater variation means the data are more spread out — a larger sample is needed to reliably distinguish meaningful patterns from noise and to maintain statistical power. Since the number of ventilated patients has remained constant, the total population has not changed, but the increased performance variation necessitates a larger sample to draw valid conclusions. Reducing the sample (A) would decrease precision exactly when more precision is needed. Keeping it the same (C) would be insufficient given the increased variation. Reviewing every record (D) is the correct gold standard if resources allow, but the question frames this as a sampling decision — increasing the sample size is the statistically appropriate answer. Per AHRQ sample size principles and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, increased variation warrants increased sample size.

questions.text: What is the maximum time interval between data points on a run chart?
questions.explanation: One Month Per standard run chart methodology and IHI guidance, data points on a run chart should be plotted at intervals no greater than one month. This ensures sufficient temporal granularity to detect trends, shifts, and patterns in a timely manner. Intervals longer than one month (such as one quarter) reduce the sensitivity of the run chart to meaningful process changes, delaying detection of improvement or deterioration. One week (A) is acceptable and even preferable in high-volume processes but is not the maximum. One quarter (C) is too infrequent and violates the IHI run chart guideline. Per IHI run chart rules and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, one month is the established maximum data point interval.

questions.text: What is the minimum number of cases in each data point on a run chart?
questions.explanation: 25 IHI run chart methodology specifies that each data point on a run chart should be based on a minimum of 25 cases to ensure that the data point is statistically stable and meaningful. Fewer than 25 cases per data point introduces excessive random variation at the individual data point level, making it difficult to distinguish true signals from noise. A single case (A) per data point is far too unstable. Ten cases (B) is insufficient for reliable statistical inference. Per IHI run chart rules and CPHQ Health Data Analytics domain standards, 25 cases per data point is the established minimum.

questions.text: A 700-bed acute care facility receives 40% of its admissions from the emergency department (ED). Quality problems, especially wait time, were expressed by patients, family members, and physicians. Which tool should the ED team use first in the investigational phase of the improvement process?
questions.explanation: Flow chart The investigational phase of the improvement process begins with understanding the current process before analyzing data or variation. A flow chart maps the current state of the ED patient flow — from arrival through triage, assessment, treatment, and disposition — revealing where delays, handoff failures, and inefficiencies exist in the actual process. This is the essential first step: you cannot improve what you do not understand. A histogram (A) displays frequency distributions but requires data already collected and analyzed. A control chart (B) monitors process variation over time — appropriate after the process is mapped and data are being tracked. A Pareto chart (D) prioritizes causes of problems — but causes cannot be prioritized until the process is understood and data are collected. Per IHI Model for Improvement, DMAIC methodology, and CPHQ performance improvement standards, process mapping (flow chart) is always the first investigational tool.

questions.text: In comparing the percentage of falls with injuries in calendar year 2012 between facilities that use restraints and those that do not, which chart should be used?
questions.explanation: Bar chart The task is to compare a percentage (falls with injuries) across two discrete categorical groups (facilities using restraints vs. those that do not). A bar chart is designed precisely for this purpose — comparing a quantitative value across distinct categories, making group differences visually clear. A line chart (A) displays trends over time for continuous data — not appropriate for a single-year comparison between two groups. A pie chart (C) shows proportions of a whole — it does not effectively communicate comparisons between separate groups. A scatter plot (D) displays the relationship between two continuous variables — not appropriate for comparing percentages across two categorical groups. Per CPHQ data analytics standards and basic data visualization principles, the bar chart is the correct tool for comparing values across categorical groups.

questions.text: Which of the following display formats is best used to evaluate the number of ear infections, urinary tract infections, and conjunctivitis experienced by individuals served in a group home?
questions.explanation: Bar chart The question presents three distinct categorical infection types (ear infections, UTIs, conjunctivitis) and asks for the best tool to display the count or frequency of each. A bar chart is the correct tool for comparing discrete categories — each infection type is a separate category, and the bar chart allows clear visual comparison of their frequencies. A line graph (A) displays trends over time, not categorical comparisons. A histogram (C) displays the frequency distribution of a single continuous variable across intervals — it is not designed for distinct categorical comparisons. A control chart (D) monitors process variation over time — not appropriate for categorical frequency comparison. Per CPHQ data analytics standards and data visualization best practices, the bar chart is correct for comparing counts across distinct categories.

questions.text: A line graph may be transformed into a run chart by

options.a: Determining the range of the data

questions.explanation: Drawing in the median measurement A run chart is a line graph with one critical addition: a center line drawn at the median of the data. The median line is what transforms a simple time-series line graph into a run chart — it is the reference line against which run chart rules (shifts, trends, runs) are applied. Without the median line, there is no statistical basis for applying run chart analysis rules. Determining range (A) is a calculation, not a visual transformation. Changing the vertical scale (C) alters the appearance but does not change the chart's analytical function. Modifying the time scale (D) similarly does not transform the chart type. Per IHI run chart methodology and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, the defining transformation from line graph to run chart is adding the median line.

questions.text: The monthly rate of resident falls in the past 12 months was plotted on a control chart. All data points are within the control limits but the last data point falls exactly on the upper control limit. The improvement team should conclude that

options.a: The process is in statistical control
options.b: The process is out of statistical control
options.c: More data points are needed to determine whether the process is in statistical control
options.d: Other statistical techniques should be used to determine whether the process is in statistical control

questions.explanation: The process is in statistical control A data point that falls exactly on the upper control limit is still within the control limits — it has not exceeded them. The rule for special cause variation requires a point to fall beyond (outside) the control limits, not exactly on them. Since all 12 data points are within or on the control limits and no other special cause rules are violated (no trends, shifts, or patterns described), the process is in statistical control. This is a precision-knowledge question designed to test exact understanding of the "beyond the limit" rule. Per Shewhart SPC rules, IHI control chart interpretation guidelines, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, a point on — but not beyond — the control limit does not constitute a signal of special cause variation.

questions.text: The first step in collecting meaningful data is

options.a: Establishing the goals of data collection

questions.explanation: Establishing the goals of data collection Before any data collection activity begins, the team must first clearly define what they are trying to accomplish — what questions they need to answer, what decisions the data will inform, and what improvement they are trying to drive. Without established goals, data collection lacks direction and may produce data that cannot answer the questions that matter. Developing operational definitions (B) is the critical second step — once goals are set, each data element must be precisely defined. Planning for data consistency (C) and evaluating resources (D) are subsequent steps in the planning sequence. Per IHI measurement science, AHRQ data quality frameworks, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, goal-setting is the foundational first step that determines everything that follows in data collection planning.

questions.text: As an external consultant, you have completed a gap analysis of an acute care facility that is preparing for TJC accreditation. Which of the following charts will you use to summarize your findings in six of the chapters of standards for the Hospital Accreditation Program?
questions.explanation: Radar chart A radar chart (also called a spider chart or web chart) is specifically designed to display performance across multiple dimensions or categories simultaneously, making it ideal for summarizing compliance status across multiple chapters of accreditation standards. Each chapter becomes an axis of the radar chart, and the organization's gap (degree of non-compliance) is plotted on each axis — producing a visual profile that immediately communicates relative strengths and weaknesses across all six chapters at once. A line chart (A) displays trends over time. A bar chart (C) compares values across categories but is less effective than a radar chart for multi-dimensional comparative profiles. A Pareto chart (D) ranks categories by frequency for prioritization — useful but not optimal for multi-chapter accreditation gap display. Per TJC accreditation preparation methodology and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, the radar chart is the optimal tool for multi-domain gap analysis presentation.

questions.text: An emergency department tracks wait times from patient arrival to physician assessment. Data are reported using a run chart. Which of the following demonstrates a true statistical increase in treatment delays?

options.c: A zigzag pattern of 10 data points
options.d: Data points close to the mean line

questions.explanation: 6 consecutive ascending data points On a run chart, a trend (sustained directional movement) signals a true statistical change in the process. The question asks about an increase in treatment delays, so ascending (increasing) data points are required. Option A (6 consecutive ascending points) is the best available answer — it represents directional movement upward. Option B (7 consecutive descending points) would signal a decrease (improvement), not an increase in delays. Option C (zigzag pattern) represents common cause variation — no directional signal. Option D (points close to the mean) represents a stable, well-performing process. Per IHI run chart methodology and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, a sustained ascending trend signals a true statistical increase.

questions.text: Which of the following sampling technique involves selecting the medical record of every fifth patient undergoing cardiovascular bypass?
questions.explanation: Systematic Systematic sampling selects every nth element from a population — in this case, every fifth patient undergoing cardiovascular bypass. This is the textbook definition of systematic sampling: a fixed sampling interval applied consistently across a defined population. Convenience sampling (A) selects whoever is available or accessible — not a fixed interval. Stratified sampling (C) divides the population into subgroups (strata) and samples from each stratum — not a fixed interval selection. Simple random sampling (D) gives every member an equal and independent chance of selection through a random process — not a fixed interval. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and AHRQ sampling methodology guidelines, fixed-interval selection (every nth case) is the defining characteristic of systematic sampling.

questions.text: Which of the following tools should be used to record patient and practitioner specific data?
questions.explanation: Spreadsheet Patient- and practitioner-specific data involves individual-level records with multiple data fields (patient ID, dates, practitioner name, procedure, outcome, etc.) — this type of structured, granular, case-level data is recorded and organized in a spreadsheet or database. A flowchart (A) maps process steps — it does not store individual case data. Graphs (B) display summarized or aggregated data — they do not record raw individual data. A histogram (C) displays frequency distributions of aggregated data — again, not a data recording tool. A spreadsheet is the appropriate tool for capturing, organizing, and storing individual patient and practitioner data fields for subsequent analysis. Per CPHQ data analytics domain competencies and standard health informatics practice, spreadsheets are the foundational data recording tool for case-level clinical data.

questions.text: When a case manager wants to demonstrate length of stay data that depicts both common cause and special cause variation, which of the following should be used?
questions.explanation: Shewhart chart The Shewhart chart (control chart) is the only tool among the options that simultaneously displays both common cause variation (data points within control limits — the normal process noise) and special cause variation (data points outside control limits or exhibiting non-random patterns). This dual display capability is the defining feature of the control chart and is exactly what a case manager needs to demonstrate LOS data in its full analytical context. A Pareto chart (A) ranks categories by frequency — it does not display variation types. A scatter plot (B) shows relationships between two variables — not time-based variation. A frequency plot (D) shows distribution — it cannot distinguish common from special cause variation. Per Shewhart's SPC methodology, IHI control chart guidance, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, the Shewhart chart is the only tool that displays both variation types.

questions.text: Which of the following is a typical size for a customer focus group?
questions.explanation: 8 to 12 The standard size for a customer focus group in healthcare quality and market research is 8 to 12 participants. This range is large enough to generate diverse perspectives and rich discussion, while small enough for the moderator to manage the conversation and ensure all participants can contribute meaningfully. Groups of 1–3 (A) or 3–5 (B) are too small to generate the diversity of opinion that makes focus groups valuable. Groups of 15–20 (D) are too large — conversations become difficult to manage, some participants are silenced, and the quality of qualitative insight deteriorates. Per CPHQ quality leadership and customer feedback standards, NCQA and IHI patient experience methodology, and focus group research best practices, 8–12 participants is the established optimal size.

questions.text: The success of a customer focus group rests principally on the:
questions.explanation: Skill of the moderator The moderator's skill is the single most critical determinant of focus group success. A skilled moderator creates psychological safety, draws out quieter participants, prevents dominant voices from skewing the discussion, keeps the conversation on topic, probes for depth without leading responses, and synthesizes emerging themes in real time. Without skilled moderation, even an optimally sized group with engaged participants will produce biased or superficial data. Group size (A) matters but is secondary to moderation quality. Meeting length (B) is a logistical parameter. The opinions of the group (C) are the raw material — but they cannot be productively captured without skilled facilitation. Per IHI patient experience methodology, NCQA member engagement standards, and focus group research best practices, moderator skill is universally identified as the primary success factor.

questions.text: Managing data and assisting with mathematical calculations is the best description of:
questions.explanation: Spreadsheet A spreadsheet application (such as Microsoft Excel) is specifically designed to organize, store, and manipulate data, perform mathematical calculations (formulas, functions, statistical analyses), and manage structured data sets. This dual capability — data management plus mathematical calculation — is the defining description of a spreadsheet. A database (A) stores and retrieves data but is primarily a data management tool without the built-in mathematical calculation interface of a spreadsheet. Graphics software (B) creates visual displays but does not manage or calculate data. A word processor (D) handles text documents — it has no meaningful data management or calculation function. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and standard health informatics competencies, the spreadsheet is the tool described.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of nominal data?
questions.explanation: Pre-op, Post-op Nominal data consists of categories that have no inherent order or ranking — they are simply labels or names. Pre-op and Post-op are mutually exclusive categorical labels with no quantitative relationship or inherent rank between them — one is not "more than" the other. AS, BS, MS, PhD (B) represents ordinal data — these educational degrees have a clear progressive hierarchy. Temperature (C) is interval or ratio data — a continuous measurement. Mass (D) is ratio data — a continuous measurement with a true zero. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and standard measurement theory, nominal data is defined by categories without order, and Pre-op/Post-op is the correct example.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of ordinal data?
questions.explanation: AS, BS, MS, PhD Ordinal data has categories with a meaningful, inherent rank order, but the intervals between categories are not necessarily equal. AS, BS, MS, PhD represents a clear progressive hierarchy of academic degrees — each level is "higher" than the previous — but the "distance" between each level is not mathematically equal. Pre-op/Post-op (A) is nominal — categories without rank. Temperature (C) is interval data — equal intervals, no true zero (on Celsius/Fahrenheit scales). Mass (D) is ratio data — equal intervals with a true zero. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and measurement theory, ordinal data is defined by ranked categories with unequal intervals, and academic degrees are the textbook example.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of ratio data?
questions.explanation: Mass Ratio data has all the properties of interval data (equal intervals, numerical values) plus a true and meaningful zero point — zero means the complete absence of the attribute being measured. Mass (weight) has a true zero: zero mass means no mass exists. This true zero point allows ratio statements such as "10 kg is twice 5 kg." Temperature on Celsius or Fahrenheit scales (C) is interval data — zero degrees does not mean absence of temperature (0°C is not the absence of heat). Pre-op/Post-op (A) is nominal. AS/BS/MS/PhD (B) is ordinal. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and measurement theory, ratio data requires a true zero point, and mass is the correct example.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of Interval data?
questions.explanation: Temperature Interval data has equal, meaningful intervals between values but lacks a true zero point. Temperature on the Celsius or Fahrenheit scale is the classic example: the difference between 10°C and 20°C is the same as between 20°C and 30°C (equal intervals), but 0°C does not mean the absence of temperature — it is an arbitrary reference point. Therefore, ratio statements ("20°C is twice as hot as 10°C") are not valid. Mass (D) is ratio data — it has a true zero. Pre-op/Post-op (A) is nominal. AS/BS/MS/PhD (B) is ordinal. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and measurement theory, temperature (Celsius/Fahrenheit) is the canonical example of interval data.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a synonym for count data?
questions.explanation: Discrete Count data refers to data collected by counting whole-number occurrences of events — the number of medication errors, patient falls, or infections. This is synonymous with discrete data, which consists of countable, whole-number values that cannot be subdivided into meaningful fractions (you cannot have 2.7 falls). Analog data (A) refers to continuous signal representation — not a data measurement type in this context. Continuous data (B) is the opposite of discrete: it can take any value within a range, including fractions and decimals (blood pressure, temperature, weight). Variable data (D) is a broad term encompassing both discrete and continuous data. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards, IHI measurement guides, and basic biostatistics, discrete data is the correct synonym for count data.

questions.text: The sampling of 5% or 30 cases, whichever is greater, is an example of sampling
questions.explanation: Quota Quota sampling sets a predetermined number or proportion of cases to be selected — in this instance, a quota of 5% of the total population or 30 cases (whichever is the larger number). This is the defining characteristic of quota sampling: specifying in advance the quantity or proportion of cases to be reviewed. Convenience sampling (A) selects based on availability, not a predetermined quota. Expert sampling (B) selects individuals based on specialized knowledge or expertise. Purposive sampling (C) selects cases based on specific characteristics relevant to the study purpose. The 5%/30 rule is a recognized standard in healthcare quality review programs (including TJC and NCQA review frameworks) and is classically defined as quota sampling. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards, this sampling rule is the textbook definition of quota sampling.

questions.text: The test used to analyze the difference between 2 means is the:
questions.explanation: T-test The t-test (Student's t-test) is specifically designed to test whether there is a statistically significant difference between the means of two groups. This is its primary and defining application. Chi-square (A) is used for categorical data — it tests associations between categorical variables, not differences between means. Multiple regression analysis (B) examines the relationship between one dependent variable and multiple independent variables — it does not test differences between two means. Regression analysis (C) examines relationships between variables and predicts outcomes — not a test of mean differences. Per AHRQ biostatistics principles, CPHQ Health Data Analytics domain standards, and standard inferential statistics, the t-test is the correct and definitive answer for comparing two means.

questions.text: If you want to predict IV site infiltration based on osmolarity of the IV solution and the addition of potassium to the IV, you should use:
questions.explanation: Multiple regression analysis The scenario involves predicting one outcome variable (IV site infiltration) from two independent predictor variables (osmolarity of the IV solution AND addition of potassium). When there are two or more independent variables predicting a single dependent variable, multiple regression analysis is the correct statistical method — it quantifies the contribution of each predictor while controlling for the others. Simple regression analysis (C) handles one predictor and one outcome — insufficient when two predictors are involved. Chi-square (A) is for categorical associations, not prediction from continuous variables. T-test (D) compares two group means — not applicable to a multi-variable prediction model. Per AHRQ research methods standards and CPHQ data analytics domain competencies, multiple regression is the correct tool when predicting an outcome from multiple independent variables simultaneously.

questions.text: Which test is often used by quality managers when data is counted, not measured?
questions.explanation: Chi-square The chi-square test is specifically designed for categorical/count data — data that is counted (number of events, frequencies, proportions) rather than measured on a continuous scale. Quality managers frequently use chi-square to test whether observed counts of events (medication errors by shift, infection rates by unit, compliance rates by department) differ significantly from expected counts, or to test associations between categorical variables. T-test (D) is for continuous measured data (means). Multiple regression (B) and regression analysis (C) are for continuous variable relationships and prediction. Per AHRQ biostatistics guidance, IHI measurement methodology, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, chi-square is the go-to test for counted (categorical) data in quality management.

questions.text: Which of the following is the best confidence interval?
questions.explanation: 0.99 A higher confidence interval means the interval will contain the true population parameter with greater certainty across repeated sampling. A 99% confidence interval (0.99) provides the highest level of certainty among the options — it means the researcher can be 99% confident the true value lies within the calculated interval. While 0.95 (B) is the most commonly used confidence level in clinical research by convention, "best" in the context of this question means the highest level of statistical confidence. 0.9 (C) and 0.85 (D) provide progressively less certainty. Note: a higher confidence interval comes with wider bounds (less precision), but for the purpose of this question, "best" refers to the level of confidence provided. Per AHRQ research standards and CPHQ data analytics domain competencies, 0.99 provides the greatest confidence.

questions.text: Historically, when the level of significance has been below [this value], researchers have rejected the null and declared their results statistically significant.
questions.explanation: 0.05 The threshold of p < 0.05 (alpha = 0.05) is the historically established and universally recognized significance threshold in clinical and healthcare research. When the calculated p-value falls below 0.05, researchers reject the null hypothesis and declare results statistically significant. This convention was introduced by Ronald Fisher and has been the standard in biomedical research for decades. 0.01 (A) is a more stringent threshold used in some contexts. 0.02 (B) and 0.1 (D) are not standard thresholds. Per AHRQ research methodology, IHI measurement science, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, p < 0.05 is the historical and conventional threshold for statistical significance.

questions.text: A freeform generation of ideas best describes:
questions.explanation: Brainstorming Brainstorming is specifically characterized by freeform, unconstrained, spontaneous generation of ideas — all ideas are recorded without judgment, evaluation, or discussion during the generation phase. This "freeform" quality is the defining feature that distinguishes brainstorming from other group idea-generation methods. The Delphi technique (B) is a structured, iterative method using anonymous expert input and feedback rounds — it is the opposite of freeform. Motivating (C) is a leadership behavior, not an idea-generation technique. The Nominal Group Technique (D) is a structured process in which participants silently write ideas individually before sharing and voting — it is semi-structured, not freeform. Per CPHQ performance improvement facilitation standards and Osborn's brainstorming methodology, freeform generation is the defining characteristic of brainstorming. SECTION 2: HDA ADDITIONAL QUESTIONS — PART A (Questions 1–22)

questions.text: Primary purpose of an information management system is to allow an organization to:
questions.explanation: Evaluate data The primary purpose of an information management system in healthcare is to collect, organize, store, and make data accessible so that it can be evaluated to support decision-making, performance monitoring, and quality improvement. While saving time (A) and reducing cost (C) are secondary benefits of efficient information management, they are operational advantages, not the primary purpose. Centralizing demographics (B) is a specific function within an information system, not its overarching purpose. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards, AHRQ health information standards, and IHI knowledge management frameworks, the primary purpose of any organizational information management system is to enable data evaluation for informed decision-making.

questions.text: For which of the following is process capability BEST used?

options.a: Identifying if a process is having the intended effect
options.b: Focusing a team on the best thing to do
options.c: Narrowing down options through a systematic approach of comparison
options.d: Determining if a process meets established specifications

questions.explanation: Determining if a process meets established specifications Process capability analysis is specifically designed to measure the extent to which a process consistently produces output that meets predetermined specifications or requirements — expressed through capability indices such as Cp and Cpk. It answers the question: "Is this process capable of meeting its specifications?" Identifying if a process is having the intended effect (A) is the domain of outcome measurement and evaluation. Focusing a team on the best thing to do (B) describes prioritization tools like Pareto analysis. Narrowing down options through comparison (C) describes decision-making matrices or multivoting tools. Per Six Sigma DMAIC methodology, IHI SPC frameworks, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, process capability is exclusively about specification conformance.

questions.text: A healthcare quality professional in the organization wants to measure the success of a corrective action plan with 95% confidence level. The average daily census is 1000 patients per day. The best sampling technique is to review:

options.a: Review 100% of all active records on one day of past month
options.b: Review 10% of all discharge records for the past quarter
options.c: Estimate the percentage of records to be reviewed using an accepted statistical formula appropriate for the population
options.d: Identify 30% of all records that failed preliminary care plan compliance review

questions.explanation: Estimate the percentage of records to be reviewed using an accepted statistical formula appropriate for the population When measuring at a defined confidence level (95%), the correct approach is to calculate the statistically appropriate sample size using a validated sample size formula that accounts for the population size, desired confidence level, acceptable margin of error, and estimated event rate. This ensures the sample is neither wastefully large nor underpowered. Reviewing 100% of active records on one day (A) is a census approach for a single day — not targeted at measuring a corrective action plan's effect over time. Reviewing 10% of discharges (B) is an arbitrary percentage without statistical grounding. Identifying 30% of failed records (D) is a purposive subset of non-compliant cases — it introduces severe selection bias. Per AHRQ sample size methodology, NQF measurement standards, and CPHQ data analytics domain competencies, statistically derived sample sizes are the gold standard for confidence-level-driven evaluations.

questions.text: The average daily census at the organization is 1000 patients. The most accurate and efficient sampling technique for this study would be:

options.a: Review 100% of all active records on one day of past month
options.b: Review 10% of all discharge records for the past quarter
options.c: Review all records that uses statistical analysis methods
options.d: Identify 30% of all records that failed preliminary care plan compliance review

questions.explanation: Review all records that uses statistical analysis methods The most accurate and efficient sampling technique for a population of 1000 patients at a defined confidence level is to apply accepted statistical analysis methods to determine the appropriate sample size — using formulas such as those from Cochran or AHRQ that account for population size, confidence level, and precision requirements. This maximizes accuracy while minimizing the number of records reviewed (efficiency). Reviewing 100% of records on one day (A) is a census, not a sample, and captures only a single-day snapshot. Reviewing 10% of discharge records (B) is an arbitrary percentage. Reviewing 30% of failed records (D) introduces selection bias by focusing only on non-compliant cases. Per AHRQ sampling methodology, NQF data quality standards, and CPHQ data analytics standards, statistically derived sampling using validated methods is the most accurate and efficient approach.

questions.text: Graphs differ from narrative data, because it can demonstrate.
questions.explanation: Both Graphs are superior to narrative data in their ability to demonstrate both trends (patterns of change over time, visible through the slope and direction of data lines) and analysis (the visual comparison, distribution, and relationships in the data that support analytical conclusions). Narrative data alone describes findings in words, but lacks the visual capacity to make trends immediately apparent or to present multivariable analytical relationships. A graph with a trend line shows the direction of change at a glance; a bar chart visually analyzes comparisons between groups. Neither trend alone nor analysis alone captures the full advantage of graphical data display. Per IHI data visualization principles and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, graphs enable both trend detection and analytical presentation — making "both" the correct answer.

questions.text: After team training of data review, evaluation of team learning may be one of the following:
questions.explanation: Interpretation of data The ultimate test of whether a team has successfully learned from data review training is their ability to interpret data — to look at a chart, graph, or dataset and draw accurate, meaningful, evidence-based conclusions. Simply drawing a Pareto chart (A) or histogram (B) demonstrates tool-use competency but not analytical understanding. Tabulating results (D) is a data organization skill, not an interpretive skill. Interpretation of data — deriving meaning, identifying patterns, drawing conclusions, and connecting data to action — is the highest-order cognitive skill in data analytics and is the true measure of training effectiveness. Per Kirkpatrick's Training Evaluation Model (Level 3: behavior; Level 4: results), and CPHQ data analytics domain competencies, data interpretation is the definitive evaluation of team learning.

questions.text: Bias of measure occurs when the measure:

options.a: Produces different results on repetitive measuring
options.c: Produces data errors consistently and systematically

questions.explanation: Produces data errors consistently and systematically Measurement bias is defined as the systematic, consistent deviation of measurements from the true value — errors that go consistently in one direction rather than occurring randomly. This is distinct from random error (imprecision), which produces inconsistent results (A — which describes unreliability, not bias). A measure that produces consistent and systematic errors is biased — it is measuring something other than what it intends to measure in a predictable, directional way. Option B (measures what's intended) describes validity — the absence of bias. Option D (excludes negative cases) describes selection bias in data collection, not measurement bias per se. Per NQF measurement standards, AHRQ data quality frameworks, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, measurement bias is defined by systematic, consistent, directional error.

questions.text: Sample results are often more accurate than results based on population because

options.a: Sample could be studied more quickly than population
options.b: Probability methods could be used to estimate the error in the resulting statistics
options.d: Possibility of bias when studying population

questions.explanation: Probability methods could be used to estimate the error in the resulting statistics The counterintuitive advantage of sampling over complete population enumeration lies in the ability to quantify and control measurement error. When probability sampling methods are used, the sampling error can be calculated mathematically — providing a known, quantifiable margin of uncertainty (confidence intervals, standard errors). Complete population studies (censuses) often suffer from non-sampling errors (data entry errors, missing records, measurement inconsistencies at scale) that cannot be estimated or controlled as precisely. Studying a sample more quickly (A) and more easily (C) are practical advantages but not accuracy advantages. Bias (D) can exist in both samples and populations. Per AHRQ sampling methodology standards and CPHQ data analytics domain competencies, the quantifiability of sampling error through probability methods is the accuracy advantage of well-designed samples over full population studies.

questions.text: In special cause variation, the source of variation is:

options.a: Intermittent, unpredictable, chronic, extrinsic and assignable
options.b: Intermittent, unpredictable, unstable, extrinsic and assignable
options.c: Intermittent, inliers, unstable, extrinsic and assignable
options.d: Intermittent, unpredictable, unstable, and intrinsic and assignable

questions.explanation: Intermittent, unpredictable, unstable, extrinsic and assignable Special cause variation (also called assignable cause variation) arises from specific, identifiable causes that are not part of the normal process — it is intermittent (not always present), unpredictable (cannot be anticipated within normal process behavior), unstable (it disrupts process stability), extrinsic (originating outside the inherent process), and assignable (traceable to a specific identifiable cause that can be investigated and eliminated). Option A is incorrect because "chronic" is a characteristic of common cause variation — special cause variation is episodic, not chronic. Option C introduces "inliers" which is not a recognized characteristic of variation types. Option D states "intrinsic" which is incorrect — special causes are extrinsic to the normal process. Per Shewhart SPC theory, IHI variation classification, and CPHQ data analytics standards, Option B correctly characterizes special cause variation.

questions.text: A common cause variation is:

options.a: An intrinsic, inliers, unpredictable, chronic variation
options.b: The responsibility of the process owners
options.c: Correctable by top management and the team
options.d: An intrinsic, outlier, unpredictable, acute variation

questions.explanation: The responsibility of the process owners Common cause variation is the inherent, predictable variability built into a process — it arises from the system itself and can only be reduced by changing the system. Since the system (processes, structures, policies) is the responsibility of process owners and management, common cause variation is their domain to address. Deming established this principle: frontline workers cannot fix common cause variation because they did not design the system — only those with authority to change the system can reduce common cause variation. Option A is incorrect: common cause variation is intrinsic (correct) and chronic (correct) but not "inliers" (not a recognized term in this context) and is predictable, not unpredictable. Options C and D are inaccurate framings. Per Deming's system of profound knowledge, IHI variation theory, and CPHQ data analytics standards, common cause variation is the responsibility of process owners who control the system.

questions.text: In a population that is NOT normally distributed (Skewed), the best statistic of the following in describing this population would be:
questions.explanation: Median In a skewed distribution, the mean is pulled in the direction of the skew (toward outliers) and no longer accurately represents the "center" of the data. The median — the middle value of an ordered dataset — is resistant to the influence of outliers and extreme values, making it the superior measure of central tendency for skewed distributions. This is why median household income and median survival time are used instead of means in skewed datasets. Mode (C) is the most frequently occurring value — useful for categorical data but less informative than the median for continuous skewed distributions. Standard deviation (D) is a measure of spread, not central tendency. Per AHRQ epidemiology standards, basic biostatistics principles, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, the median is the correct measure of central tendency for skewed distributions.

questions.text: If data include patients' blood pressures, these data are categorized as:
questions.explanation: Continuous Blood pressure is a continuous variable — it is measured on a scale that can theoretically take any value within a range, including decimal fractions (e.g., 118.5 mmHg). Continuous data arises from measurement (using instruments) rather than counting. Nominal data (A) consists of unordered categories — clearly not applicable to blood pressure. Ordinal data (C) consists of ordered categories with unequal intervals — also not applicable to a measured physiological variable. Discrete data (D) consists of countable whole numbers — blood pressure is not counted but measured and can be any value within a range. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and basic measurement theory, blood pressure is continuous data.

questions.text: A hospital needs to decide whether or not to incorporate a new feature into its current services, and as a result has commissioned qualitative research that will provide detailed feedback. Specifically, the hospital would like to collect opinions from patients and other hospital customers with a wide range of experience and backgrounds. Which of the following types of assessments is most likely to be of use to the hospital?
questions.explanation: Focus group The hospital is seeking qualitative feedback from a diverse group of patients and customers with varied experiences — this is exactly the scenario for which focus groups are designed. Focus groups bring together participants with a range of backgrounds to generate rich, qualitative discussion about experiences, opinions, and needs — providing the depth and diversity of perspective that surveys cannot capture and that case studies do not provide at the group level. A case study (A) provides deep analysis of a single case — not appropriate for gathering diverse group opinions. A survey (B) collects quantitative or structured data from many respondents but lacks the depth of discussion and the ability to explore emerging themes. Team analysis (C) is an internal process, not a customer feedback method. Per CPHQ data analytics and customer-focused quality standards, focus groups are the designated tool for collecting qualitative opinions from diverse customer groups.

questions.text: A patient care unit has a high fall rate. The Patient Safety Committee wants to know more about the data. A patient safety professional displays the number of falls and where they occurred. Which of the following is the best way to show this to the committee?
questions.explanation: Bar chart The question asks for a display showing the number of falls (frequency) and where they occurred (location — a categorical variable). A bar chart is precisely designed to display counts or frequencies across discrete categories — in this case, fall counts by location (room, hallway, bathroom, etc.). This gives the Patient Safety Committee an immediate visual understanding of which locations have the highest fall burden. A scatter diagram (A) shows the relationship between two continuous variables — not appropriate for counts by location. A run chart (C) tracks a single metric over time — not for categorical location comparison. A pie graph (D) shows proportions of a whole — less effective than a bar chart for identifying which specific locations need attention. Per CPHQ data analytics and patient safety domain standards, the bar chart is the correct tool for categorical frequency display.

questions.text: Which type of chart uses to identify variation for the aggregated data?
questions.explanation: Control chart The control chart is the tool specifically designed to identify variation in aggregated data over time — distinguishing common cause variation (expected, within control limits) from special cause variation (unexpected signals outside control limits). For aggregated data (data summarized at regular intervals — monthly infection rates, quarterly readmission rates, etc.), the control chart displays the variation pattern and signals when the process is out of control. A pie chart (A) shows proportions — not variation. A bar chart (B) compares categories — not a variation analysis tool. A histogram (D) shows distribution of a dataset — it displays variation within a static snapshot but does not track variation in aggregated data over time. Per IHI SPC methodology and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, the control chart is the variation identification tool for aggregated time-series data.

questions.text: When sampling a population for data collection, consider

options.a: The size of the sample — the larger, the better
options.b: The time period being sampled — the longer, the better
options.c: If the collection mechanism is biased toward improving an outcome
options.d: If the characteristics of the sample are the same as the target population

questions.explanation: If the characteristics of the sample are the same as the target population The most critical consideration in sampling is representativeness — whether the sample accurately reflects the characteristics of the population it is intended to represent. A sample that shares the key characteristics of the target population produces valid, generalizable results. A larger sample (A) improves statistical precision but is not the primary consideration — a large biased sample is worse than a smaller representative one. A longer time period (B) may capture more variation but does not guarantee representativeness. A biased collection mechanism (C) must be avoided, but this option describes a pitfall to avoid rather than a primary consideration to "consider" in sampling design. Per AHRQ sampling standards, NQF measurement principles, and CPHQ data analytics domain competencies, representativeness is the foundational sampling consideration.

questions.text: Which of the following is a nominal variable?
questions.explanation: Religion Nominal variables are categorical variables with no inherent order or rank — they are simply labels or names for categories. Religion is a nominal variable: Catholic, Muslim, Hindu, Jewish, etc. are categories with no quantitative relationship or rank between them. Age (A) is a ratio variable — a continuous, measurable quantity with a true zero. Blood pressure (C) is a continuous/ratio variable — a physiological measurement. Occupation (D) could initially seem nominal, but it is typically treated as nominal; however, Religion is the clearest and most unambiguous example of a nominal variable from this list. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and standard measurement theory, religion is the correct nominal variable in this set.

questions.text: In statistical procedures, generally as sample size increases:

options.a: The standard error increases in size
options.b: The standard error decreases in size
options.c: The standard error remains the same
options.d: The standard error is a constant that is not related to sample size

questions.explanation: The standard error decreases in size The standard error of the mean (SEM) is calculated as the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size (SEM = SD/√n). As sample size (n) increases, √n increases, making the denominator larger — which makes the SEM smaller. This means that larger samples produce more precise estimates of the population mean, with narrower confidence intervals. This is the mathematical basis for why larger samples provide more reliable estimates. Options A, C, and D directly contradict this fundamental statistical relationship. Per AHRQ biostatistics principles, CPHQ data analytics domain standards, and standard inferential statistics, standard error decreases as sample size increases.

questions.text: You are doing research on hospital personnel including orderlies, technicians, nurses, pharmacists, and doctors. You want to be sure you draw a sample that has cases in each of the personnel categories. An appropriate sampling method would be:
questions.explanation: Stratified random sampling Stratified random sampling divides the population into predefined subgroups (strata) — in this case, the five personnel categories — and then randomly samples from each stratum. This guarantees representation from every category, which is exactly what the researcher requires. Simple random sampling (A) gives every individual an equal chance of selection but may not guarantee that all personnel categories are represented — small categories could be missed entirely. Cluster sampling (C) selects groups (clusters) rather than individuals and samples all individuals within selected clusters — appropriate for geographically dispersed populations, not for ensuring category representation. Convenience sampling (D) selects based on availability — introducing bias and providing no guarantee of category coverage. Per AHRQ sampling methodology and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, stratified random sampling is the correct method when representation across defined subgroups is required.

questions.text: Measures of Central tendency describe

options.a: The extent to which the data points are scattered
options.c: The average distance of any variable in the data set from the mean
options.d: The typical or middle data point

questions.explanation: The typical or middle data point Measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) describe the center of a data distribution — the typical, representative, or middle value around which the data cluster. Option A describes measures of dispersion (variance, standard deviation, range) — not central tendency. Option B describes data visualization tools — not a statistical measure. Option C describes the average distance from the mean, which is the concept underlying standard deviation — a measure of dispersion, not central tendency. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and basic descriptive statistics, central tendency measures describe the typical or central data point.

questions.text: A sampling interval of 10 was used to select a sample from a population of 1200. How many elements are to be in the sample?
questions.explanation: 120 Calculation: In systematic sampling, the sample size is calculated as: Population ÷ Sampling interval = 1200 ÷ 10 = 120 elements. A sampling interval of 10 means every 10th element is selected from the population. With a population of 1200 and an interval of 10, exactly 120 elements will be selected (1200/10 = 120). This is the standard systematic sampling calculation. Option A (12) would result from dividing by 100. Option C (1200) is the entire population — a census, not a sample. Option D (1180) = 1200 − 20, which has no basis in sampling calculation. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and systematic sampling methodology, the correct calculation yields 120 elements.

questions.text: Generally, large quantity data sets are summarized using
questions.explanation: Descriptive Statistics Descriptive statistics (means, medians, frequencies, percentages, standard deviations, ranges) are the tools used to summarize and describe large datasets in a concise, meaningful way. They condense large quantities of data into interpretable summary measures that communicate the essential characteristics of the dataset. Inferential statistics (B) are used to draw conclusions or make inferences about a population from a sample — they are not primarily summarizing tools. Reports (C) and newsletters (D) are communication formats that may contain descriptive statistics, but they are not the statistical method used to summarize data. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and basic biostatistics, descriptive statistics is the correct answer for summarizing large data sets. SECTION 3: HDA ADDITIONAL QUESTIONS — PART B (Questions 23–48)

questions.text: Standard deviation is

options.a: The spread of the data from the highest to lowest numbers
options.b: The average distance of observations from the mean
options.c: A sort of data that are symmetrically distributed
options.d: The middle value of 50% reference point of all occurrences

questions.explanation: The average distance of observations from the mean Standard deviation is a measure of dispersion that quantifies how far, on average, the individual data points in a dataset are from the mean. More precisely, it is the square root of the average squared deviations from the mean — but conceptually, it represents the average distance of observations from the mean. Option A describes the range (highest minus lowest), not standard deviation. Option C describes a normal distribution, not standard deviation. Option D describes the median (the value at the 50th percentile). Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and basic descriptive statistics, standard deviation is correctly defined as the average distance of observations from the mean.

questions.text: Failure free operation over time can be used to describe which of the following characters of a measuring procedure?
questions.explanation: Reliability Reliability of a measuring procedure refers to its consistency and stability — the ability to produce the same results repeatedly under the same conditions over time. "Failure-free operation over time" describes a measure that continues to perform consistently without breaking down or producing inconsistent results — this is reliability. Validity (B) refers to whether the measure accurately measures what it is intended to measure — not about consistency over time. Sensitivity (C) is the ability of a test to correctly identify true positives. Specificity (D) is the ability to correctly identify true negatives. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards, NQF measurement science, and standard psychometrics, reliability is defined by consistent, stable, failure-free performance over time.

questions.text: The most effective data collection tools follow the [actual flow] of patient care and medical records documentation, whether the data are collected retrospectively or prospectively.
questions.explanation: Actual flow The most effective data collection tools are designed to mirror and follow the actual flow of patient care and documentation — meaning they capture data in the sequence and manner in which clinical events and documentation actually occur. Tools designed around the actual clinical workflow minimize missing data, reduce burden on collectors, and produce data that is clinically accurate and contextually relevant. Chart review (B) is a retrospective data collection method — not the design principle for effective data collection tools. Data analysis (C) is the process that follows collection. A registration system (D) captures administrative intake data — not a design principle for clinical data collection tools. Per AHRQ data collection methodology and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, alignment with actual patient care flow is the defining principle of effective data collection tool design.

questions.text: A healthcare organization has experienced an increase in errors related to patient identification. The patient safety specialist has been asked to provide data showing what type of errors are occurring and at what frequency. Which of the following is the best tool to effectively demonstrate this?
questions.explanation: Pareto chart The question asks for a tool that shows both the type of errors and their frequency — and specifically which types are occurring most often. The Pareto chart is designed precisely for this: it displays categories of errors (types) along the x-axis and their frequency (count) on the y-axis, ranked from most to least frequent, with a cumulative percentage line. This immediately answers both questions — what types of errors are occurring and at what frequency — and identifies which error types account for the majority of occurrences (the vital few, per the 80/20 rule). A run chart (B) tracks a single metric over time — it does not categorize error types. A scatter diagram (C) shows relationships between two variables.
