Per AHRQ research methodology, basic biostatistics, and CPHQ data analytics standards, sampling is the process of learning about a population from a drawn sample.

questions.text: The basic objective of a sample is to draw _______ about the population from which such sample is drawn.
questions.explanation: The fundamental objective of sampling is to make inferences — statistically grounded conclusions drawn from sample data that are generalized to the population. While "conclusion" (A) is related, "inference" is the precise statistical term for the process of reasoning from sample to population. Characteristics (B) are attributes observed in the sample. Parameters (D) are population values estimated by sample statistics — they are what we infer, not what we draw. Per AHRQ research methodology, basic biostatistics, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, making inferences about the population is the defining objective of sampling.

questions.text: In _______ type of classification, the data is grouped together according to some distinguished characteristic or attribute, such as religion, sex, age, national origin, and so on.
questions.explanation: Qualitative classification groups data by non-numerical attributes or characteristics — such as religion, sex, national origin, or diagnosis category. These are categorical distinctions, not numerical measurements. Quantitative classification (A) groups data by numerical values or ranges. Chronological classification (B) groups data by time periods. Per basic biostatistics, AHRQ data classification standards, and CPHQ data analytics domain knowledge, grouping by distinguishing attributes is qualitative classification.

questions.text: For a sample to be truly representative of the population, it must truly be _____________.
questions.explanation: A truly representative sample must be randomly selected — meaning every member of the population has an equal and independent probability of being included. Random selection eliminates systematic bias and ensures the sample reflects the population's characteristics. Fixed (A), specific (C), and casual (D) are not recognized sampling quality standards and do not guarantee representativeness. Per AHRQ sampling methodology, basic biostatistics, and CPHQ data analytics standards, randomness is the essential property of a representative sample.

questions.text: A _________ sample is obtained by selecting convenient population units.
questions.explanation: A convenience sample is obtained by selecting units that are readily available and accessible — the defining feature being ease of access rather than any randomization or stratification principle. Random sampling (A) requires equal probability of selection. Quota sampling (B) sets predetermined subgroup counts. Stratified sampling (C) divides the population into subgroups before random selection. Per AHRQ research methodology, basic biostatistics, and CPHQ data analytics standards, selecting convenient population units defines a convenience sample.

questions.text: The upper and lower control limits in a control chart are

options.a: Used to identify the distribution of data
options.b: Calculated by using the collected data

questions.explanation: Control limits in a Shewhart control chart are statistically calculated from the actual collected process data — specifically derived from the process mean and standard deviation (typically ±3 sigma). They are not preset thresholds (C) — this is the critical distinction between control limits and specification limits. They are not used to identify distribution (A — that is a histogram). Per IHI SPC methodology, Shewhart's original control chart theory, and CPHQ data analytics standards, control limits are calculated from collected data.

questions.text: The upper and lower limits of a control chart are
questions.explanation: Control chart limits are derived from actual process measurement data — calculated as the process mean ±3 standard deviations (or the appropriate sigma multiple for the chart type). They are not projected from future requirements (B), derived from special cause variation (C — special cause variation is what the chart detects, not what defines the limits), or set by external regulatory bodies (D — this describes specification limits, not control limits). Per Shewhart's SPC theory, IHI improvement tools, and CPHQ data analytics standards, control limits are calculated from actual process measurements.

questions.text: To assess compliance with quality standards, a healthcare organization needs
questions.explanation: Compliance with quality standards can only be assessed validly if data is collected in a standardized, consistent manner — using defined data elements, operational definitions, and uniform collection protocols. Governing body approval (B) is a governance function, not a measurement prerequisite. A dedicated team (C) may help but is not the essential requirement. Electronic analysis software (D) is a tool, not a prerequisite. Per NQF measurement standards, AHRQ data quality guidelines, and CPHQ data analytics domain requirements, standardized data collection is the foundational requirement for compliance assessment.

questions.text: When reporting infection control indicators to a governing body, a healthcare quality professional should demonstrate improvement with which of the following tools?
questions.explanation: When demonstrating improvement over time to a governing body, a run chart is the appropriate tool — it plots infection control data points sequentially over time, making trends, shifts, and improvement trajectories visible. A frequency plot/histogram (B) displays distribution at a point in time, not improvement trajectories. A pie chart (C) shows proportional composition — not suitable for demonstrating temporal improvement. A scatter plot (D) shows relationships between two variables. Per IHI governance reporting guidance, TJC Board-level quality reporting standards, and CPHQ data analytics standards, the run chart is the correct tool for demonstrating longitudinal improvement.

questions.text: Before patient outcome data can be used for benchmarking, the data should be
questions.explanation: Patient outcome data must be adjusted for severity of illness (risk-adjusted) before it can be validly used for benchmarking. Without severity adjustment, observed outcome differences between organizations may reflect case mix differences rather than true quality differences — making any comparison misleading. Organizing by age (A) or gender (D) is stratification, not adjustment. Adjusting for length of stay (B) is a utilization metric, not a severity adjustment method. Per NQF outcome measure standards, CMS risk adjustment methodology, AHRQ comparative effectiveness guidance, and CPHQ data analytics standards, severity adjustment is the required prerequisite for valid outcome benchmarking.

questions.text: Special cause variation is also known as:
questions.explanation: Assignable, extrinsic, outlier. In statistical process control (SPC), variation is classified into two types. Common cause variation is inherent, random, and intrinsic to the process — it is expected background noise. Special cause variation, by contrast, is assignable — it can be traced to a specific, identifiable, external cause that does not belong to the normal process distribution. The term "outlier" correctly characterizes a special cause data point as falling outside the expected process limits. Option A incorrectly combines "assignable" (correct) with "intrinsic" and "noise" — both of which describe common cause variation. Option B is inaccurate on all descriptors. Per IHI statistical process control methodology, Shewhart's original control chart theory, and CPHQ Health Data Analytics domain standards, special cause variation is defined as assignable, extrinsic, and outlier in nature.

questions.text: In statistical process control, it is important first to
questions.explanation: Eliminate assignable cause of variation. In SPC methodology, the sequence of improvement is deliberate and non-negotiable. Before any process improvement is attempted, all special cause (assignable) variation must first be identified and eliminated. A process with special cause variation is said to be "out of control" — its behavior is unpredictable, and any attempt to improve it while special causes remain will be futile or misleading. Only after a process is stable (special causes removed) can you meaningfully work to reduce common cause variation and improve the process average. Eliminating random (common cause) variation (B) is the second step, not the first. Prioritizing causes (C) is vague and not the SPC-mandated first step. Eliminating all variation (D) is neither possible nor desirable — common cause variation is inherent in all processes. Per Shewhart and Deming's SPC theory and IHI improvement frameworks, eliminating assignable cause is always the first step in SPC.

questions.text: A small, rural hospital wishes to evaluate customer satisfaction using a survey. The organization has four patient care units, an emergency department, and an ambulatory unit. Which of the following survey methods provides the most reliable information?

options.a: A random sample of 20% of annual discharges/visits per unit
options.b: A random sample of 5% of annual discharges/visits per unit
options.c: All discharges/visits in January and July
options.d: All discharges/visits of customers with a last name beginning with the letters A–E

questions.explanation: A random sample of 20% of annual discharges/visits per unit. For a satisfaction survey to yield reliable and representative data across multiple distinct care units, the sampling method must be both adequately sized and unit-specific. A 20% random sample drawn from each unit provides sufficient statistical power to detect meaningful differences in satisfaction across units, while the unit-stratified approach ensures all care areas are proportionally represented. A 5% sample (B) is likely to be too small for subgroup-level analysis across six units. Sampling only January and July (C) introduces seasonal bias — satisfaction patterns may differ in summer versus winter or by census variation. Selecting patients by last name (D) is a systematic approach but could introduce unintended demographic bias if alphabetical distribution is uneven. Per AHRQ survey methodology guidance and CPHQ Health Data Analytics domain standards, stratified random sampling at adequate proportions per unit is the most reliable method for multi-unit satisfaction measurement.

questions.text: According to epidemiological theory, the rate of new cases of transfusion reaction since the previous year would be termed
questions.explanation: An incidence rate. Incidence rate measures the rate of new cases of a condition or event occurring within a defined population over a specified time period. The question explicitly states "new cases since the previous year" — this time-bounded emergence of new events is the textbook definition of incidence. Prevalence (C) measures all existing cases (both new and old) at a given point in time or over a period — it does not distinguish new from existing. A numerator (A) is a component of a rate calculation, not a rate itself. A denominator (B) is likewise a component, not a rate. Per CDC epidemiology principles, AHRQ surveillance definitions, and CPHQ Health Data Analytics domain standards, the rate of new cases over time is definitionally an incidence rate.

questions.text: The use of regression analysis to help determine relationships between groups of numbers is most closely associated with which graphic display technique?
questions.explanation: Scatter diagram. Regression analysis examines the statistical relationship between two or more variables — specifically whether and how changes in one variable predict changes in another. The scatter diagram is the graphical tool that displays this relationship visually, plotting paired data points to reveal the direction, strength, and form of the association between variables. The regression line is plotted on a scatter diagram. Frequency distribution (A) and histogram (D) display the distribution of a single variable. A line graph (C) shows trends over time for one variable. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and basic biostatistics, scatter diagram is the graphic technique associated with regression analysis and correlation assessment.

questions.text: The QI team is responsible for determining whether the data demonstrates special or common cause variation. Of the following, what is the best display option to use?
questions.explanation: Control chart. The control chart (Shewhart chart) is specifically designed to distinguish between common cause variation (natural process noise within control limits) and special cause variation (signals outside control limits or exhibiting non-random patterns). A run chart can display trends and may show some signals, but it does not have statistically derived upper and lower control limits — making it insufficient for definitively classifying variation type. A Pareto chart (B) ranks causes by frequency — it does not display variation over time. A scatter diagram (C) displays relationships between two variables. Only the control chart provides the statistical framework (3-sigma limits, run rules) needed to make the common vs. special cause determination with confidence. Per IHI SPC methodology, Shewhart's original work, and CPHQ data analytics standards, the control chart is the definitive tool for variation classification.

questions.text: Which of the following descriptions correctly correlate with continuous data?

options.a: Variables, counted, categorized, percentages, means, t test
options.b: Counted, categorized, measured, variables, means, t test
options.c: Discrete, counted, categorized, percentages, chi-square, whole numbers
options.d: Attributes, counted, measured, discrete, chi-square, means

questions.explanation: however, the correct framing requires clarification. Upon independent analysis: None of the options is perfectly constructed, but B is the least incorrect for continuous data in that it includes "measured," "variables," and "means, t test" — which are genuinely continuous data characteristics. The contaminating terms "counted" and "categorized" in option B are discrete data descriptors that should not appear here. The correct characteristics of continuous data are: measured (not counted), variables data, infinite values on a continuum, analyzed using means and standard deviation, and tested with parametric tests such as the t-test. Options C and D explicitly feature discrete/attribute data markers (chi-square, whole numbers, counted, categorical). Option A mixes continuous and discrete descriptors. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and basic measurement theory, continuous data is measured, expressed as variables, and analyzed with means and t-tests — making B the best available answer despite its imperfect construction.

questions.text: Which of the following sampling techniques involves selecting the medical record of every fifth patient undergoing cardiovascular bypass?
questions.explanation: Systematic. Systematic sampling selects every nth element from a list or sequence — in this case, every fifth patient. The selection interval is fixed and predetermined. Convenience sampling (A) selects based on availability. Stratified sampling (C) divides the population into subgroups and samples from each. Simple random sampling (D) gives every member an equal, independent chance of selection. The defining characteristic of systematic sampling is the fixed interval selection rule — "every fifth" is the canonical example. Per AHRQ sampling methodology and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, selecting every nth case is definitionally systematic sampling.

questions.text: An emergency department trends wait times from patient arrival to physician assessment. Data are reported using run chart. Which of the following demonstrate a true statistical increase in treatment delay?

options.c: A zigzag pattern of 10 data points
options.d: Data points close to the mean line

questions.explanation: 6 consecutive ascending data points. In run chart analysis, a trend is defined as six or more consecutive data points all moving in the same direction (all ascending or all descending) — this signals a statistically meaningful directional shift in the process, not random variation. Six consecutive ascending points on a wait-time run chart indicate a true, non-random increase in treatment delay. Seven consecutive descending points (B) would indicate a decreasing trend — in the context of wait times increasing, this is the wrong direction. A zigzag pattern (C) is random oscillation — no trend signal. Data points close to the mean (D) indicate a stable, well-centered process — the opposite of a problem. Per IHI run chart rules, Nelson run rules, and CPHQ data analytics standards, six consecutive points in one direction constitutes a trend signal.

questions.text: Prior to plotting a line graph, a healthcare quality professional should first
questions.explanation: Identify the parameters. Before any graphical display is constructed, the foundational first step is to identify the parameters — the variables, data elements, time frames, and scope that the graph is intended to display. Without parameter identification, you cannot meaningfully define axes, calculate means, or develop a legend, because you do not yet know what you are measuring or displaying. Defining axis measurements (B) is the second step, dependent on knowing the parameters. Calculating the mean (A) is a computational step that follows data collection and parameter definition. Developing a legend (D) is a final formatting step.

questions.text: Which of the following are measures of central tendency?

options.b: Standard deviation, variance and standard error
options.c: Grouped data, bell curve and distribution

questions.explanation: Mean, median, and mode. The three measures of central tendency in descriptive statistics are the mean (arithmetic average), median (middle value), and mode (most frequently occurring value). These three statistics describe where the center of a data distribution lies. Standard deviation, variance, and standard error (B) are measures of dispersion — they describe spread, not center. Grouped data, bell curve, and distribution (C) are data organization and shape concepts, not central tendency measures. Correlation, regression, and t-test (D) are inferential statistical techniques. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and basic biostatistics, mean, median, and mode are the universally recognized measures of central tendency.

questions.text: Sample include all available data in the area
questions.explanation: Convenience. The description "all available data in the area" — meaning whoever or whatever is accessible and present — is the defining characteristic of convenience sampling. Convenience sampling does not apply predetermined proportions (quota), does not divide into subgroups (stratified random), and does not select based on specific characteristics (purposive). It simply uses what is available. This is the operational definition of convenience sampling across all statistical methodology references. Per AHRQ sampling methodology and CPHQ data analytics standards, availability-based sampling in a defined area is convenience sampling.

questions.text: Released reports revealed that appendectomy rate is 50% of new admissions to a male surgical ward. What else is needed to interpret this report?

options.d: Number of days within the study period

questions.explanation: Sample size. A rate of 50% is meaningless without knowing the denominator on which it is based. A 50% appendectomy rate from 4 admissions (2 patients) is statistically trivial; the same rate from 400 admissions is highly significant and actionable. Sample size is the essential contextual element needed to determine the reliability, significance, and interpretability of any reported rate. Ethnicity (B) may be relevant for equity analysis but is not necessary to interpret the basic rate. Sources of data (C) matter for validity assessment but are secondary to understanding the rate's magnitude. Number of days (D) defines the time frame but does not change the rate's interpretation the way sample size does. Per AHRQ measurement principles and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, rates must always be accompanied by the sample size (denominator) to be interpretable.

questions.text: Upper control limit and lower control limit is
questions.explanation: Actual process measure. The upper control limit (UCL) and lower control limit (LCL) on a control chart are calculated from the actual process data itself — specifically from the mean and standard deviation of the process measurements (typically ±3 standard deviations from the mean). They are not derived from special cause variation (A) — special cause variation is what the control limits are designed to detect, not their source. They are not external benchmarks (C) set by outside bodies. The control limits are entirely data-derived from the process being measured, making "actual process measure" the correct descriptor. Per Shewhart's control chart theory, IHI SPC guidance, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, UCL and LCL are calculated from actual process measurements.

questions.text: A valid data collection should incorporate
questions.explanation: The definition of data elements. Validity of a data collection tool requires that each data element be precisely and operationally defined so that all collectors interpret and record elements consistently. Without definitions, inter-rater variability destroys data reliability and validity. Graphic presentation (A) is a reporting tool, not a collection validity requirement. A minimum of 20 elements (C) is an arbitrary number with no basis in measurement science. Allowing variance of interpretation (D) actively undermines validity — it is the opposite of what a valid tool requires. Per NQF measurement standards, AHRQ data quality guidelines, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, operational definitions of data elements are the foundational validity requirement.

questions.text: Rate of cesarean section over 5 years — best display
questions.explanation: Control chart. Displaying a rate measured repeatedly over a five-year period is a time-series problem — the data has a temporal dimension and the goal is to understand how the rate is behaving over time, whether it is stable or changing, and whether any changes represent special cause signals or common cause variation. The control chart is the ideal tool: it plots the rate over time with statistically derived control limits, distinguishing meaningful change from random fluctuation. A bar chart (A) could display annual rates side by side but cannot distinguish common from special cause variation. A Pareto chart (C) ranks categories by frequency — it is not a time-series tool. A fishbone (D) is a cause-analysis tool, not a data display tool. Per IHI SPC methodology and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, time-series rate data over multiple periods is best displayed on a control chart.

questions.text: When assessing an emergency room, the best strategy for data collection is
questions.explanation: Continuous sampling. Emergency departments present a unique data collection challenge: patient volumes fluctuate dramatically by time of day, day of week, and season; acuity is highly variable; and the nature of ED care means patients arrive unpredictably and may be discharged rapidly. Continuous sampling — collecting data on every case or patient across all time periods — is the best strategy because it captures the full variability of ED operations and does not miss high-acuity periods or off-peak times that other sampling strategies might systematically exclude. Cluster sampling (A) samples predefined groups — it could miss important time-based variation. Matched random sampling (C) is used in case-control research designs, not operational quality data collection. Accidental sampling (D) is synonymous with convenience sampling — collecting whoever is available — which introduces availability bias in an ED where the most critical patients may be unavailable for data collection. Per AHRQ emergency department quality measurement guidance and CPHQ data collection methodology, continuous sampling is the recommended strategy for high-variability, unpredictable care settings.

questions.text: In data collection, Qualitative data are to Quantitative data as
questions.explanation: Opinion are to facts. Qualitative data captures subjective, descriptive, non-numerical information — perceptions, opinions, experiences, attitudes, and narratives. Quantitative data captures objective, numerical, measurable information — counts, rates, frequencies, and measurable outcomes. The analogy "opinions are to facts" correctly maps this distinction: opinions are subjective and interpretive (qualitative), while facts are objective and measurable (quantitative). Option C (attitudes to deeds) is partially plausible but is a weaker analogy — attitudes are qualitative, but "deeds" (actions) are behavioral, not inherently quantitative. Option B is meaningless in this context. Option D (actions to outcomes) maps process to result, not data type to data type. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and research methodology, the qualitative/quantitative distinction is most precisely captured by the opinion/fact analogy.

questions.text: The upper and lower control limits of a process control chart are three standard deviations from the mean. A data point that falls outside these limits

options.a: Will be found 5% of the time even if the process is in statistical control
options.b: Will be found 5% of the time even if the process is out of statistical control
options.c: Indicates the presence of a sentinel event
options.d: Is a signal for further investigation

questions.explanation: Is a signal for further investigation. When a data point falls outside the ±3 standard deviation control limits on a control chart, it is classified as a special cause signal — an indication that something non-random has occurred that warrants investigation. The correct and complete response is that it requires investigation to determine whether a true special cause exists and what drove it. Option A is statistically incorrect: with ±3 sigma limits, approximately 99.73% of data falls within limits for a normally distributed process — meaning only about 0.27% of points (not 5%) would fall outside by chance. The 5% false-alarm rate applies to ±2 sigma limits, not ±3 sigma. Option B is also incorrect for the same statistical reason. Option C is wrong: a data point outside control limits is a process signal, not a sentinel event — sentinel events are defined clinical patient safety events, not statistical signals. Per Shewhart SPC theory, IHI control chart methodology, and CPHQ data analytics standards, a point outside control limits is a signal for further investigation.

questions.text: In which of the following scenarios is rule-based sampling most appropriate?

options.b: Assessing compliance to the time-out procedure

questions.explanation: Assessing compliance to the time-out procedure. Rule-based sampling — also called criterion-based or triggered sampling — collects data according to a predefined rule or trigger condition rather than randomly or continuously. Assessing time-out compliance is ideally suited to rule-based sampling because a specific, identifiable event (every surgical procedure) triggers the data collection. The rule is: "For every procedure in which a time-out is required, assess compliance." This ensures every relevant event is captured according to a consistent rule. Customer feedback (A) is better collected through surveys or focus groups. Patient falls (C) are tracked through occurrence reporting — all falls are reported, not rule-sampled. Laboratory machine functional testing (D) follows calibration schedules, which is protocol-based but not "rule-based sampling" in the QI sense. Per CPHQ data collection methodology and TJC Universal Protocol monitoring standards, rule-based sampling is the appropriate strategy for procedure-specific compliance monitoring.

questions.text: What is the most likely effect of tampering when dealing with control charts?

options.a: Reducing variation when the process is stable
options.b: Increasing variation when the process is stable
options.c: Failing to recognize special cause variation when it is present
options.d: Falsely identifying special cause variation when none exists

questions.explanation: Increasing variation when the process is stable. Tampering refers to making adjustments to a stable process in response to common cause variation — treating normal process noise as if it were a special cause signal requiring correction. Deming demonstrated that tampering with a stable process invariably increases variation rather than reduces it — the classic illustration being his funnel experiment, in which repeated adjustments to a stable system caused the output to drift progressively further from target. A stable process should be left alone; adjustments should only be made when a genuine special cause signal is detected. Option A is the opposite of what tampering does. Option C (failing to recognize special cause) is the error of treating special cause as common cause — the opposite of tampering. Option D (falsely identifying special cause when none exists) is the error leading to tampering but is not the effect of tampering itself. Per Deming's SPC theory, IHI process control methodology, and CPHQ data analytics standards, the consequence of tampering is increased variation in a stable process.

questions.text: An acute care facility recently revised its clinical protocol for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia. It has since experienced greater variation in monthly staff performance. The number of ventilated patients per month has remained approximately the same. When sampling medical records for the monthly review, how should the organization adjust the sample size?

options.c: Keep the sample size the same
options.d: Review the medical record of each ventilated patient until variation is reduced

questions.explanation: Increase the sample size. When variation in performance increases, the statistical requirement for an adequate sample size also increases. Greater variation means a larger spread of data, which requires a larger sample to precisely estimate the true population mean and to detect whether performance changes are real or simply due to sampling error. The volume of ventilated patients has not changed, so the population is the same — but the increased variability within that population necessitates a larger sample to maintain the same level of measurement precision. Reducing the sample size (A) would worsen measurement precision at the worst possible time. Keeping it the same (C) would reduce the statistical power of the monthly review. Reviewing every record until variation reduces (D) conflates sampling strategy with outcome — you do not review records until a result is achieved; you review a sufficient sample to measure what is happening. Per AHRQ statistical sampling guidance and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, increased process variation is an indication to increase sample size.

questions.text: Which of the following is a typical size for a customer focus group?
questions.explanation: 8 to 12. The established optimal size for a customer focus group in qualitative research methodology is 8 to 12 participants. This range is large enough to generate diverse perspectives and rich discussion, but small enough for the moderator to manage effectively and for all participants to contribute meaningfully. Groups smaller than 8 (A, B) may produce limited perspective diversity and are vulnerable to domination by one or two voices. Groups of 15 to 20 (D) are too large for effective facilitation — side conversations emerge, not all participants speak, and group dynamics become difficult to manage. Per AHRQ qualitative research methodology, IHI patient experience measurement guidance, and standard focus group design principles, 8–12 participants is the recognized optimal range.

questions.text: The success of a customer focus group rests principally on the:
questions.explanation: Skill of the moderator. While group size matters (see Q23), it is the moderator's skill that is the single most critical determinant of focus group success. A skilled moderator creates psychological safety, draws out quieter participants, manages dominant voices, keeps discussion on topic, probes for depth beyond surface responses, and synthesizes emerging themes — all without introducing bias. Without skilled moderation, even an optimally sized group will produce shallow, biased, or incomplete data. Group size (A) is important but secondary to moderation quality. Meeting length (B) and group opinions (C) are contextual factors, not primary success determinants. Per AHRQ qualitative research standards, IHI customer insight methodology, and standard focus group design literature, moderator skill is universally identified as the principal determinant of focus group quality and success.

questions.text: Which test is often used by quality managers when data is counted, not measured?
questions.explanation: Chi-square. The chi-square test is the standard statistical test for categorical (counted, attribute) data — it tests whether observed frequencies differ significantly from expected frequencies, or whether two categorical variables are associated. When data is counted (e.g., number of patients who did or did not fall, number of procedures with or without complications), chi-square is the appropriate test. T-test (D) is used for continuous (measured) data comparing means. Regression analysis (C) and multiple regression (B) examine relationships between continuous variables. The key distinction: counted data = chi-square; measured/continuous data = t-test or regression. Per CPHQ data analytics domain standards and AHRQ statistical methodology guidance, chi-square is the go-to test for counted, categorical healthcare quality data.

questions.text: Which of the following sampling techniques selects participants based on their availability in a certain place during a specific time frame?
questions.explanation: Convenience. Convenience sampling selects participants based on their accessibility and availability at a specific location and time. This is the defining characteristic — selection is driven by practicality rather than randomization or predetermined structure. Per AHRQ and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, availability-based participant selection in a specific place and time is convenience sampling by definition.

questions.text: The results from a Nominal Group Technique session can be presented as 5 points
questions.explanation: Bar chart. The Nominal Group Technique (NGT) is a structured group decision-making and prioritization process in which participants independently rank or score options, and scores are totaled to produce a prioritized list. The output is a ranked set of items with associated point totals — this is categorical data with associated numerical scores. A bar chart is the correct display tool: it can show each option on the x-axis with its total score on the y-axis, clearly communicating the priority ranking. A pie chart (B) displays proportional parts of a whole — it does not convey ranking or comparative scores effectively for NGT output. A run chart (C) tracks a single variable over time. A scatter plot (D) displays relationships between two continuous variables. Per CPHQ performance improvement facilitation standards and quality tool selection guidelines, bar charts are used to display NGT results because they clearly show the ranked priority scores.

questions.text: Tools used to compare the current level with desired level
questions.explanation: Radar (Gap). The question describes a gap analysis function — comparing where the organization currently is against where it wants to be (desired level). A radar chart (also called a spider diagram or gap analysis chart) is specifically designed to display multiple dimensions of current performance against target or desired levels simultaneously, making the gaps visually apparent across multiple domains. A flow chart (B) maps process steps — it does not compare current vs. desired performance levels. A workflow (A) describes process sequencing. A Pareto chart (C) ranks problems by frequency — it does not compare current vs. desired states. Per CPHQ performance improvement and strategic planning tool standards, the radar/gap chart is the recognized tool for multi-dimensional current vs. desired state comparison.

questions.text: Relationships are best displayed by a

options.a: Flowchart, cause and effect diagram, scatter diagram
options.c: Pie chart, prioritization matrix, Pareto chart
options.d: Flowchart, cause and effect diagram, check sheet

questions.explanation: Flowchart, cause and effect diagram, scatter diagram. This question asks which combination of tools best displays relationships. A scatter diagram directly displays the statistical relationship between two variables. A cause and effect (Ishikawa/fishbone) diagram displays the relationship between causes and a specific effect/problem. A flowchart displays the relationships between sequential process steps and decision points. Together, these three tools span the spectrum of relationship visualization: statistical relationships, causal relationships, and sequential/process relationships. Option B includes a run chart (trend over time, not relationships) and a table (data storage, not relationship display). Option C includes a Pareto chart (prioritization/ranking) and a pie chart (proportional composition). Option D substitutes a check sheet (data collection tool) for the scatter diagram, losing the statistical relationship display capability. Per CPHQ quality improvement tool standards, A is the combination most oriented toward displaying relationships of different types.

questions.text: The Pareto rule is which of the following?

options.b: 80% Of the problems have 20% of the impact
options.c: 20% Of the problems have 80% of the impact
options.d: 20% Of the costs reap 80% of the benefit

questions.explanation: 20% of the problems have 80% of the impact. The Pareto Principle, derived from Vilfredo Pareto's observation and popularized in quality management by Joseph Juran, states that approximately 20% of causes are responsible for 80% of effects — or in the quality context, 20% of problems account for 80% of the impact, harm, or defects. This is the foundational principle behind the Pareto chart and the concept of focusing improvement efforts on the "vital few" causes rather than the "trivial many." Option B inverts the principle. Option A is a fabricated statement. Option D misapplies the rule to costs and benefits without basis. Per Juran's Quality Handbook, IHI Pareto analysis methodology, and CPHQ performance improvement domain standards, the Pareto rule is precisely stated as: 20% of causes produce 80% of the effects.

questions.text: Focus groups provide patient/customer input or feedback. What type of information do they offer?
questions.explanation: Qualitative. Focus groups are a qualitative research method. They gather rich, narrative, descriptive data about perceptions, experiences, attitudes, and opinions — data that cannot be reduced to numbers or measurements. The purpose of a focus group is to explore the "why" and "how" behind patient or customer experiences, not to produce counts, rates, or statistical measures. Quantitative (B) refers to numerical, measurable data produced by surveys with Likert scales, counts, or rates. "Measured" (C) is synonymous with quantitative. "Opinionated" (D) is not a recognized data type category. Per AHRQ qualitative methods guidance, IHI patient experience methodology, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, focus groups are definitionally a qualitative data collection method.

questions.text: The first step in conducting an epidemiological study is to

options.b: Determine which statistical test to use
options.d: Formulate the question to be answered

questions.explanation: Formulate the question to be answered. Every epidemiological study begins with a precisely formulated research question — the question defines what is being studied, in what population, over what time period, and with what expected relationships. Without a clear question, no other step can be executed correctly: data collection is unfocused, statistical tests cannot be chosen, and instruments cannot be designed. The research question is the compass for every subsequent decision. Collecting data (A) is a downstream step. Choosing statistical tests (B) depends on the question and data type. Developing the tool (C) depends on knowing what you need to measure. Per CDC epidemiology principles, AHRQ research methodology, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, formulating the research question is universally recognized as the first step in any epidemiological study.

questions.text: The result of the customer survey: the mean score was calculated with each item. Weight was applied to rank each item in order of importance to the customer. Which of the following has the highest weighted mean score?
questions.explanation: Calculation — Weighted Mean Score = Mean × Weight: A: 3 × 0.9 = 2.70 B: 4 × 0.8 = 3.20 C: 5 × 0.7 = 3.50 D: 6 × 0.6 = 3.60 Mean 6 and weight 0.6. A weighted mean score is calculated by multiplying each item's mean score by its assigned weight. The weight coefficient reflects the relative importance of that item to the customer — a higher weight means the item matters more. The weighted mean score (mean × weight) integrates both the performance score and the importance level into a single composite value, allowing meaningful prioritization across items. Working through each option: A yields 2.70, B yields 3.20, C yields 3.50, and D yields 3.60. Although Option D has the lowest weight (0.6) and Option A has the highest weight (0.9), Option D's substantially higher mean score (6) produces the largest product. This is a deliberate trap in the question design — students who focus only on the weight column will incorrectly select A. The correct approach is always to calculate the product for every option before selecting. Option D at 3.60 is the highest weighted mean score. Per CPHQ Health Data Analytics domain standards and standard weighted scoring methodology, the item with the highest mean × weight product is correctly identified as the top priority item.

questions.text: Within Statistical analysis, the mean might also be described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Average. The mean is the arithmetic average of a set of values — the sum of all values divided by the number of values. In everyday language and in introductory statistical communication, the mean and the average are synonymous terms. Probability (A) is the likelihood of an event occurring — a separate statistical concept. Dispersion (C) refers to the spread or variability of data (standard deviation, variance, range) — not central tendency. Coefficient (D) is a multiplier or statistical measure of relationship strength (e.g., correlation coefficient) — not synonymous with the mean. Per basic biostatistics, CPHQ data analytics domain standards, and statistical terminology, the mean is correctly described as the average.

questions.text: All the following are factors that influence sample size EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Power analysis. This is a nuanced EXCEPT question. The factors that legitimately influence sample size determination include: the purpose of the research (what question is being answered and what precision is needed), the population size (larger populations may permit smaller proportional samples), and the level of confidence desired (higher confidence levels require larger samples to achieve narrower confidence intervals). Power analysis is not a separate "factor" that influences sample size — it is the statistical method used to calculate the required sample size. It is the tool, not the influencing factor. In other words, you perform a power analysis to determine what sample size you need given the other factors. Per AHRQ statistical sampling methodology and CPHQ data analytics standards, power analysis is the calculation process, while purpose, population size, and confidence level are the inputs to that calculation.

questions.text: The upper and lower limits of a control chart are
questions.explanation: Calculated from actual process measurements. Control limits on a Shewhart control chart are computed directly from the data generated by the process being monitored — specifically from the process mean and standard deviation, set at ±3 standard deviations from the mean. They are empirically derived from what the process actually produces, not from external standards, benchmarks, or projections. Projecting future requirements (B) describes target-setting or specification limits — not control limits. Derived from special cause variation (C) is incorrect — special cause variation is what the limits are designed to detect, not their source. External regulatory standards (D) may define specification limits or performance thresholds, but they do not define statistical control limits. This concept was also tested at Q14 in this batch. Per Shewhart's original control chart theory, IHI SPC guidance, and CPHQ data analytics standards, control limits are calculated from actual process data.

questions.text: Choosing a small number of items to represent characteristics of the whole is an example of
questions.explanation: Sampling methodology. The precise definition of sampling is selecting a subset (small number of items) from a larger population (the whole) in order to draw inferences about the characteristics of that population. This is sampling methodology by definition. Outlier identification (B) is the process of detecting anomalous data points — not selecting a representative subset. Statistical significance (C) refers to the probability that an observed result is not due to chance — it is a test result, not a data collection strategy. Benchmarking (D) involves comparing organizational performance against external standards or peers — not subset selection. Per AHRQ sampling methodology, CPHQ data analytics domain standards, and basic research methodology, selecting a small number of items to represent the whole is the definition of sampling.

questions.text: Which of the following should a healthcare plan use to collect satisfaction data from its health plan members?

options.a: Data collected through questionnaires or surveys
options.b: Claims data obtained from healthcare payors
options.c: Disease data obtained from disease registries
options.d: Data collected from the electronic health record

questions.explanation: Data collected through questionnaires or surveys. Member satisfaction is a subjective, experiential construct — it captures how members perceive and feel about their healthcare experience. The only way to directly measure satisfaction is to ask members directly through questionnaires or surveys. This is the methodological foundation of CAHPS (Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems), the gold standard satisfaction instrument endorsed by AHRQ and CMS for health plan measurement. Claims data (B) captures utilization and billing — it does not capture member experience. Disease registries (C) track clinical outcomes, not satisfaction. EHR data (D) contains clinical documentation — not patient satisfaction assessments. Per NCQA HEDIS technical specifications, CMS member experience measurement standards, and CPHQ data analytics domain principles, surveys and questionnaires are the validated instruments for health plan member satisfaction data.

questions.text: Each department in a hospital self-monitors and reports hand hygiene data each quarter. Results typically fall within the 58–72% range, with the exception of Respiratory Therapy, which consistently reports 100% compliance. Which of the following steps should a healthcare quality professional take next?

options.a: Provide remedial hand hygiene training for the lowest scoring departments
options.b: Recognize the Respiratory Therapy department for its outstanding compliance
options.c: Validate that the Respiratory Therapy results are accurate
options.d: Require departments not achieving at least 95% compliance to develop corrective action plans

questions.explanation: Validate that the Respiratory Therapy results are accurate. When one unit in a system consistently reports a result that is dramatically and implausibly different from all other comparable units — in this case, 100% compliance when every other department ranges from 58–72% — the appropriate quality response is to validate the accuracy of that outlier data before acting on it. A 100% compliance rate in hand hygiene is extraordinarily rare and statistically implausible for any healthcare department operating at scale. The most likely explanations are: self-reporting bias, social desirability bias, measurement error, inadequate observation sample, or data fabrication. Acting on unvalidated outlier data — whether to reward (B) or to use as a benchmark — risks embedding a false standard. Remedial training for lowest scorers (A) and corrective action plans (D) address underperformers but bypass the data integrity issue. Per AHRQ data quality standards, IHI measurement integrity principles, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, implausible outlier results must be validated before any action is taken based on them.

questions.text: When reporting infection control indicators to a governing body, a healthcare quality professional should demonstrate improvement with which of the following tools?
questions.explanation: Run chart. When reporting improvement in infection control indicators to a governing body, the goal is to demonstrate change over time — showing that performance has shifted in a positive direction as a result of improvement efforts. The run chart is the ideal tool for this purpose: it plots the indicator over time, makes trend lines visible, and can display the median and annotated change points (interventions). For governing body reporting, the run chart effectively communicates the story of improvement in a visually accessible format. A frequency plot (B) displays distribution of data values — not trend over time. A pie chart (C) shows proportional composition at a point in time — not improvement trajectories. A scatter plot (D) displays relationships between two variables. Per IHI measurement and reporting guidance, TJC performance reporting standards, and CPHQ data display methodology, the run chart is the standard tool for demonstrating improvement over time to organizational leadership.

questions.text: Before patient outcome data can be used for benchmarking, the data should be
questions.explanation: Adjusted for severity of illness. This question parallels Q14 from the prior session (severity adjustment for LOS benchmarking) and applies the same principle to patient outcome data broadly. Before comparing patient outcomes across organizations, providers, or time periods, the data must be risk- or severity-adjusted. Without severity adjustment, differences in outcomes between organizations may simply reflect differences in patient acuity (case mix) rather than differences in quality of care. Organizing by age (A) or gender (D) is demographic stratification — useful for subgroup analysis but not a validity requirement for benchmarking. Adjusting for length of stay (B) would be circular for outcome benchmarking — LOS is itself often an outcome measure, not a confounding variable to adjust for. Per NQF, CMS, AHRQ, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, severity-of-illness adjustment is the mandatory prerequisite for valid outcome data benchmarking.

questions.text: A healthcare quality professional receives complaints from numerous patients that the registration process is inefficient. Which of the following should be used to best identify customer expectations, perceptions, and improvement opportunities?
questions.explanation: Focus group with patients. When the goal is to understand customer expectations, perceptions, and improvement opportunities — particularly around a process they have experienced firsthand — a focus group with those patients is the most powerful method. Focus groups allow patients to describe their experiences in depth, respond to each other's observations, and surface themes that a structured survey would not capture. The registration process is a complex, multi-step patient-facing experience where the nuance of perception matters enormously. A telephone survey (A) can reach more patients but produces shallower, structured data. A written survey of staff (C) or interviews with staff (D) capture the provider perspective, not the patient/customer perspective — they cannot identify patient perceptions or expectations. Per AHRQ qualitative methods guidance, IHI patient experience principles, and CPHQ data collection standards, focus groups with patients are the optimal method for capturing rich, experiential customer insight about a specific process.

questions.text: A criterion is considered valid if it

options.b: Does not change with changes in technology
options.c: Is applicable to many groups and settings
options.d: Measures what it is intended to measure

questions.explanation: Measures what it is intended to measure. Validity, in measurement science, has a precise and universal definition: a measure is valid if it measures what it is intended to measure. This is content validity at its most fundamental. Option A describes reliability — consistently yielding the same results is the definition of reliability (repeatability), not validity. A measure can be reliable (consistent) without being valid (measuring the right thing). Option B (not changing with technology) describes stability or durability — not a validity criterion. Option C (applicable to many groups and settings) describes generalizability — a desirable but separate attribute from validity. Per NQF measurement standards, AHRQ measurement science guidance, and CPHQ data analytics domain standards, validity is definitionally whether a criterion or instrument measures what it is designed to measure.
